title: Daniel's 70 Weeks

keyTerms.d: The Hebrew word translated “weeks” is literally “sevens.” Almost everyone, Jewish and Christian, conservative and critical, reads these as sevens of years: seventy times seven equals 490 years. The structure is 7 + 62 + 1 weeks (49 + 434 + 7 years).

The word that becomes “Messiah.” Hebrew has no capital M; the term simply means “anointed,” and in the Old Testament it can name a king, a priest, or even the pagan Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1). So Daniel 9 does not say “the Messiah” in the later technical sense. It says an anointed one comes, and then an anointed one is “cut off.”

A verb used elsewhere for violent death and judicial execution. Daniel 9 genuinely seems to expect an anointed one within the Second Temple era, and to expect him to be killed. The whole interpretive war is about who these figures are.

keyTerms.t: “The word to restore and build Jerusalem”
keyTerms.d: The clock’s starting point. Scripture records more than one Persian decree — Cyrus (c. 538 BC), Artaxerxes I to Ezra (458/457 BC), Artaxerxes I to Nehemiah (445/444 BC) — and the candidates land decades apart; Daniel 9:25 may instead refer to the divine word through Jeremiah, which is the critical default. The question is not cleanly settled.

The year-length the famous day-precise calculations need, inferred from Revelation rather than stated in Daniel. It is contested even among conservatives, and to outside critics it looks like special pleading.

A major dividing accent the Masoretes placed after “seven weeks” in verse 25, which makes the 7 and 62 two separate periods and brings the anointed one of verse 25 after only 49 years. A genuinely contested philological point — but what it changes is the identity of the figure in verse 25, not the timing of the death in verse 26.

The critical consensus that Daniel reached its final form around 165 BC, under Antiochus IV Epiphanes. On it the seventy weeks are a theological structure — ten jubilees of years answering Jeremiah’s seventy — the anointed one cut off is Onias III, murdered around 171 BC, and the desolator is Antiochus IV. It is the majority view, but not a proof.

The narrow point the ancient Jewish sources establish: Seder Olam Rabbah mapped Daniel’s seventy weeks onto the lifespan of the Second Temple, and Josephus treats Daniel as a prophet whose visions were most naturally read as pointing to the Roman desolation of the sanctuary. Neither reads Daniel 9 as Christians do — but both locate its horizon at the end of the Second Temple era, which is precisely the era of Jesus.

derive.q: Daniel 9 places the anointed one’s violent death before the destruction of the city and sanctuary — so the order of events is…?
derive.ans: in the text itself — anointed death, then ruin
derive.why: “And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary” (Daniel 9:26). Whether you read it through Onias III or through Jesus, the shape is the same: an anointed death, then ruin.

derive.q: Even its critics date the text no later than the second century BC — so its expectation of an anointed death before the sanctuary’s fall is…?
derive.ans: a striking convergence, even on the critical date
derive.why: Even at 165 BC the book predates Jesus by two centuries and still expects an anointed death before the sanctuary’s fall. For a text composed no later than the second century BC, that is a striking convergence even before anyone counts a single day.

derive.q: After Onias III’s death the sanctuary was profaned but rededicated; after Jesus’s, the city and temple were destroyed — so the terminal event fits…?
derive.why: After Onias III’s death, Antiochus’s forces sacked and burned parts of the city and profaned the sanctuary (1 Maccabees 1:31, 39), but the sanctuary itself was not destroyed and was rededicated in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52–54); after Jesus’s, the city and its temple were destroyed, by “the people of the prince” (verse 26), in AD 70.

derive.q: The day-precise count needs a particular decree, a particular punctuation, a 360-day year and an exact crucifixion date — so as proof it is…?
derive.ans: too dependent on contestable choices — retire the stopwatch
derive.why: Presenting the calculations as a knockdown “countdown to Christ” invites the charge of rigging the dials, a charge that sometimes sticks. When an argument’s persuasive force depends on hitting an exact day, being off by a day or two is not a rounding error; it is the difference between a fingerprint and a smudge.

derive.q: The Maccabean reading must name Onias III, rely on numbers that overshoot by some sixty-five to seventy years, and take the punctuation the other way — so it is…?
derive.why: The messianic reading requires real interpretive choices. But neither reading simply falls out of the text; the claim to resist is that the non-messianic reading is the effortless default and the messianic one a contrivance.

derive.q: Grant all of it: an anointed one cut off before the city and sanctuary fell. Does that, by itself, prove Jesus is the Messiah?
derive.ans: no — a suggestive strand, not a proof
derive.why: It is the kind of evidence that rewards the person already weighing the whole cloth of the case for Christ, and frustrates the person demanding a single decisive thread. Daniel 9 does not deliver a mathematical demonstration of Jesus’s messiahship.

honestState.p1: The majority of academic Old Testament scholars do not read Daniel 9 as pointing to Jesus at all. The critical consensus — represented by John J. Collins’s Hermeneia commentary, the standard scholarly commentary — holds that Daniel reached its final form around 165 BC, and reads the seventy weeks as a theological structure resolving to the Maccabean crisis. That is the majority view, but not a proof.
honestState.fairness: Three concessions are owed. The 360-day “prophetic year” is contested even among conservatives, and to outside critics it looks like special pleading. The “decree” question is not cleanly settled — Daniel 9:25 may refer to the divine word through Jeremiah, the critical default. And the two readings are not symmetrical guesses: the Maccabean reading fits the book’s own preoccupations and requires no special arithmetic, while the messianic reading requires a particular decree, a particular punctuation, and (for the day-precise version) a particular year-length. Those are real interpretive choices. But the Maccabean reading is not dial-free either: it must identify the “anointed one” who is “cut off” with Onias III, rely on its own inexact numbers (which overshoot the era they aim at by some sixty-five to seventy years), and take the same disputed punctuation the other way. Neither reading simply falls out of the text; the claim to resist is that the non-messianic reading is the effortless default and the messianic one a contrivance.
honestState.verdict: Daniel 9 does not deliver a mathematical demonstration of Jesus’s messiahship; the honest apologist retires the stopwatch. But it establishes something quieter and harder to dismiss: a text that even its critics date to no later than the second century BC announces that within the era of the rebuilt Jerusalem an anointed one would come and be “cut off,” and that the city and sanctuary would then be destroyed. Our claim is not that Daniel 9 calculates Jesus to the day. It is that Jesus is the anointed one the prophecy foresaw (arriving in the Second Temple era, anointed, and cut off, before the sanctuary’s end) and that no other candidate answers its whole shape as he does — a suggestive strand, not a proof.

order: Daniel 9 orders the events: a word to restore Jerusalem, then an anointed one comes and is cut off, then the city and sanctuary are destroyed.
The text predates Jesus, and its terminal event — the destruction of city and sanctuary — fell in AD 70, not after Onias III.
Therefore the anointed one, on Daniel’s own sequence, comes and is cut off before AD 70 — and no other candidate answers its whole shape as Jesus does.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: Daniel 9:24–27 runs from “the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem” to an anointed one who is then “cut off,” after which the city and sanctuary are destroyed. Limit: mashiach simply means “anointed” — Daniel 9 does not say “the Messiah” in the later technical sense, and the whole interpretive war is about who these figures are.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and what it does not need.
cards.a: The text predates Jesus, and its terminal event is the destruction of the city and the sanctuary, which fell in AD 70. The premise needs a text that even its critics date to no later than the second century BC — it does not need the critical date to be wrong.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That Jesus is the anointed one the prophecy foresaw (arriving in the Second Temple era, anointed, and cut off, before the sanctuary’s end), and that no other candidate answers its whole shape as he does. Not that Daniel 9 calculates Jesus to the day: it is a suggestive strand, not a proof.

cards.q: What is the key move — and why make it?
cards.a: Argue the sequence, not the day-count. Interpreters disagree over start-decrees and year-lengths, so build on the order the text itself lays out: a word to rebuild, then an anointed one, then he is cut off, then the city and sanctuary are destroyed. No 360-day gymnastics required, the rough order of magnitude being the point.

Shabuʿim is literally “sevens,” and almost everyone, Jewish and Christian, conservative and critical, reads these as sevens of years: seventy times seven, 490 years. Gabriel answers Daniel’s prayer over Jeremiah’s seventy years of exile with a far larger seventy.

cards.q: What concession is owed on the famous day-precise calculation?
cards.a: That it is too dependent on contestable choices — the decree, the punctuation, the 360-day year, the exact crucifixion date — to function as proof. The 360-day year is not stated in Daniel but imported from Revelation, and critics have pointed to technical slips. The honest apologist retires the stopwatch.

cards.q: What does Qumran show about Daniel’s date — and what does it not settle?
cards.a: Fragments of Daniel were found at Qumran, and the book was treated as authoritative scripture there soon after its supposed composition; conservatives argue that presses an uncomfortably short window, while critics judge the gap sufficient. It does not settle the date — and the argument needs only a text that even its critics date no later than the second century BC.

cards.q: Does the Masoretic accent after “seven weeks” sink the argument?
cards.a: No — it is a genuinely contested philological point, but it matters less than it first appears. Even on the Masoretic division, verse 26 still places the anointed one’s cutting-off “after the sixty-two weeks,” which follow the first seven. What the accent changes is the identity of the figure in verse 25, not the timing of the death in verse 26.

cards.q: Grant the critical date of c. 165 BC — what follows for the argument?
cards.a: It does not overturn the argument: even at 165 BC the book predates Jesus by two centuries and still expects an anointed death before the sanctuary’s fall. The late date is the majority view but not a proof — and the argument does not need it overturned.

cards.q: Why does the Maccabean reading fit a clause but not the whole?
cards.a: After Onias III’s death the city was sacked in part and the sanctuary profaned, but the sanctuary itself was not destroyed and was rededicated (1 Maccabees 4:52–54). Daniel’s terminal event is that the people of the prince “shall destroy the city and the sanctuary” — which happened only after Jesus’s death, in AD 70.

cards.q: “Collins says the numbers are simply inexact” — why does that cut both ways?
cards.a: If the author of a Maccabean Daniel was writing about events in his own lifetime, his inability to make 490 years reach cleanly from any starting point to 164 BC is itself a little awkward — he, of all people, knew when Antiochus desecrated the temple. The looseness is real, but it equally undermines any tidy this-equals-that Maccabean fulfillment.

cards.q: What do the ancient Jewish sources establish — and not establish?
cards.a: Only the narrow point: Jewish tradition itself tied Daniel 9’s clock to the end of the Second Temple era. The rabbis read the weeks non-messianically; it is no Jewish endorsement of the Christian reading. Neither source reads Daniel 9 as Christians do — but both locate its horizon at the end of the Second Temple era, the era of Jesus.

obj.q: The 70-weeks “prophecy” is tortured math — 360-day years and cherry-picked decrees, reverse-engineered onto Jesus. The precision is manufactured.
obj.model: Largely agreed about the stopwatch — which is why the argument refuses to stand on it. There is no statement in Daniel that its years are 360 days; the inference is imported from Revelation, and the day-precise calculations are too dependent on contestable choices to function as proof. The honest apologist retires the stopwatch. But drop every disputed assumption and the order of events remains in the text: an anointed one comes and is cut off, and then the city and sanctuary are destroyed — which happened in AD 70. The structural reading underneath the math — held by Calvin, Hengstenberg and Young alike — is simply that the 69 weeks run from a Persian decree to the public ministry and death of Christ in the first century AD: no 360-day gymnastics required, the rough order of magnitude being the point.

obj.q: Read in its own setting, the anointed one cut off is Onias III, murdered around 171 BC, and the desolator is Antiochus IV. The seventy weeks are ten jubilees of years — theology in the shape of a number. No Jesus required.
obj.model: That is the majority critical reading, and it deserves its full strength: it fits the book’s own preoccupations and requires no special arithmetic. But it is not dial-free either: it must identify the anointed one who is cut off with Onias III, rely on its own inexact numbers — which overshoot the era they aim at by some sixty-five to seventy years — and take the disputed punctuation the other way. And it fits a clause, not the whole: after Onias III’s death the sanctuary was profaned but not destroyed, and was rededicated in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52–54), while Daniel’s terminal event is the destruction of the city and the sanctuary. Neither reading simply falls out of the text; what to resist is the claim that the non-messianic reading is the effortless default and the messianic one a contrivance.

obj.q: The Masoretic accent splits the weeks: an anointed one after seven weeks, another sixty-two weeks later — lowercase figures, centuries apart. Your messianic reading rides on Christian punctuation.
obj.model: The punctuation dispute is real: the Masoretes placed a major dividing accent after “seven weeks,” and modern critical translations such as the NRSV follow it, while the King James and NIV traditions join the 7 and 62, following the earlier Greek versions and the Vulgate. But it matters less than it first appears. Even on the Masoretic division, verse 26 still places the anointed one’s cutting-off “after the sixty-two weeks,” which follow the first seven. What the accent changes is the identity of the figure in verse 25, not the timing of the death in verse 26.

obj.q: Even granting all that, it buys you a deadline, not an identification. Plenty of people died before AD 70.
obj.model: Correct about the argument’s scope: by itself Daniel 9 supplies a window and a profile — an anointed one, cut off, before the city and sanctuary are destroyed — not a name, and it does not deliver a mathematical demonstration of Jesus’s messiahship. What it does show is that the critics’ own candidate fits a clause, not the whole: after Onias III’s death the sanctuary was profaned but not destroyed, and was rededicated; the city and its temple were destroyed only after Jesus’s, in AD 70. That is a suggestive strand, not a proof — the kind of evidence that rewards the person already weighing the whole cloth of the case for Christ, and frustrates the person demanding a single decisive thread.

unseen.q: Daniel 9:25’s “word to restore and build Jerusalem” is the divine word through Jeremiah — the critical default — not a Persian edict. Start there and your clock has no starting gun; the 483 years land nowhere near Jesus.
unseen.model: Grant what is true in it: the decree question is not cleanly settled. The text’s “word to restore and build Jerusalem” most naturally evokes the rebuilding of the city, but Daniel 9:25 may instead refer to the divine word through Jeremiah, not any Persian edict at all, which is the critical default. That is why the honest apologist retires the stopwatch: what Daniel 9 establishes is quieter — that within the era of the rebuilt Jerusalem an anointed one would come and be “cut off,” and that the city and sanctuary would then be destroyed. Nor is the critic’s own clock clean: the Maccabean reading must rely on inexact numbers that overshoot the era they aim at by some sixty-five to seventy years. Neither reading simply falls out of the text. And Daniel’s terminal event — the destruction of the city and the sanctuary — did not follow Onias III’s death; it followed Jesus’s, in AD 70.
